scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The pogo originated in the mid-1970s London punk scene.
Sid Vicious is widely cited as its inventor, using it as a tool to mock non-punk attendees at Sex Pistols concerts.
It was conceived as an 'anti-disco' dance, rejecting the smooth, synchronized movements of the mainstream.
on_screen: Map: United Kingdom · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The pogo is performed at live music concerts.
It functions as a form of collective release and a way for the audience to engage physically with the music, fostering a sense of solidarity among participants.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The basic form involves jumping vertically on the spot.
The torso is kept rigid, arms are held stiffly at the sides, and legs are kept close together.
Dancers may also spin in the air or move around the space, depending on the intensity of the music.
Watch for Vertical Jump.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (mi2q5-Ia-RU)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Crowded, non-linear, collective.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is primarily associated with punk rock, hardcore, and heavy metal.
The music is characterized by fast tempos, aggressive guitar riffs, and driving drum beats, designed to encourage high-energy movement.
Listen for the Electric guitar, Electric bass, Drums.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 160 beats a minute.
Fast-paced, distorted electric guitars and a heavy, driving drum beat create an urgent, high-energy atmosphere that compels the listener to move.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: There is no specific costume, though early punk attire such as leather jackets or ponchos were common.
It is performed in concert venues, typically in the area in front of the stage known as the 'mosh pit'.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Sid Vicious, Shane MacGowan, and Viv Albertine are central figures associated with the early history and popularization of the pogo.
Variants include slam dancing, moshing, circle pits, and the 'wall of death,' where the crowd splits and charges at each other.
The pogo is considered the precursor to modern moshing and slam dancing.
